expansion:
The keyed answer is A. Abscess formation is the important local complication of an untreated severe bacterial infection in this region. The vignette localizes to the lacrimal gland: the course states that swelling of the lateral eyelid over the palpebral lobe produces the characteristic “S-SHAPED PTOSIS” (L10, slide 31). In its bacterial orbital-cellulitis teaching, the lecture lists “Subperiosteal abscess” among complications and notes that drainage of an orbital abscess should be considered early (L10, slide 27 and 29). Thus, suppuration with abscess formation is the relevant local progression.

The lecture’s acute dacryoadenitis slide does not itself describe a bacterial cause or abscess complication; it instead says “Idiopathic or due to viral (e.g. mumps, Epstein–Barr, cytomegalovirus” (L10, slide 31). This differs from the stem’s severe bacterial infection, but the printed key remains A.

B. Retinal detachment is wrong because it is a separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium, not the expected local consequence of an acute bacterial lacrimal-gland/orbital infection (not taken from the course material).

C. Glaucoma is wrong because glaucoma is an optic neuropathy commonly associated with raised intraocular pressure, rather than the principal local suppurative complication described here (not taken from the course material). The lecture does mention raised IOP among ocular complications of bacterial orbital cellulitis, but does not identify glaucoma as the key complication (L10, slide 27).

D. Cataract is wrong because cataract is lens opacity and does not arise as the important immediate local complication of this acute infection (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognize that an untreated severe bacterial infection with lateral upper-lid swelling and S-shaped ptosis may progress to local abscess formation.
